nameStory: The mourning cloak gets its somber name from its dark, velvety wings that resemble the black cloaks traditionally worn during periods of mourning. The pale yellow border along the wing edges looks like decorative trim on funeral attire. Interestingly, the British call this same butterfly the 'Camberwell beauty' — a much cheerier name for the exact same species!
description: The mourning cloak is one of New England's most distinctive large butterflies, with velvety dark brown to black wings bordered by a creamy yellow band. These powerful fliers are about the size of your palm when their wings are spread open. Unlike many butterflies that live just a few weeks, mourning cloaks are remarkable survivors that can live nearly a full year. You'll often see them gliding gracefully through woodlands or basking with their wings spread wide on sunny tree trunks.

idTips.label: Wing Pattern
idTips.description: Deep chocolate brown to black wings with a distinctive pale yellow border running along all wing edges, creating a striking frame-like appearance that's visible even in flight

idTips.label: Blue Spots
idTips.description: A row of iridescent blue spots runs just inside the yellow border, catching the light like tiny sapphires when the butterfly moves

idTips.label: Size and Shape
idTips.description: Large butterfly with angular wing shape and slightly ragged wing edges that feel papery to the touch if you find a deceased specimen

idTips.label: Flight Pattern
idTips.description: Strong, gliding flight with powerful wingbeats, often sailing effortlessly between trees rather than the fluttery flight of smaller butterflies

idTips.label: Wing Underside
idTips.description: When wings are folded, shows mottled gray and brown bark-like camouflage that makes them nearly invisible against tree trunks

habitat: Mourning cloaks prefer deciduous and mixed woodlands throughout New England, especially areas with willow, elm, birch, and poplar trees where their caterpillars feed. You'll often spot them along woodland edges, in parks with mature trees, and near streams or wetlands where willows grow. They're also drawn to tree sap, rotting fruit, and mud puddles in sunny forest clearings.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge from winter hibernation in March and April, often seen basking on warm rocks or tree trunks on the first sunny days. This is when they're most active and easiest to spot before leaves fully emerge.
seasonality.summer: Less commonly seen during peak summer heat, as adults become less active. Look for spiny black caterpillars with red spots feeding on willow and elm leaves in late summer.
seasonality.fall: Fresh adults from the summer generation appear in late August and September, building up fat reserves before winter. They seek out tree sap and overripe fruit to fuel up for hibernation.
seasonality.winter: Adults hibernate in tree crevices, under loose bark, or in wood piles. On warm winter days above 50°F, you might spot them briefly emerging to bask in the sun before returning to shelter.

funFact: Mourning cloaks are one of the few butterflies that actually hibernate as adults through New England's harsh winters, tucked away in tree bark crevices with natural antifreeze in their blood — making them among the first butterflies you'll see flying on warm late-winter days, sometimes even with snow still on the ground!
confusionNotes: The mourning cloak's distinctive yellow-bordered dark wings make it hard to confuse with other butterflies, but from a distance it might be mistaken for a large moth. Remember: mourning cloaks hold their wings vertically when at rest (like butterflies do), while moths typically hold wings horizontally or roof-like over their bodies.
contextualKnowledge: This butterfly goes by completely different names depending on where you are — 'mourning cloak' in North America but 'Camberwell beauty' in Britain, showing how the same species can have vastly different cultural associations. It's also Montana's state insect, chosen for its ability to survive harsh winters.
compareHints: The mourning cloak is much larger and darker than its close relative the Compton tortoiseshell, which has more orange coloration and white patches instead of the solid yellow border. While both are in the tortoiseshell group, the mourning cloak's consistent dark coloring and yellow trim make it unmistakable. The Compton tortoiseshell also has a more complex, mottled wing pattern compared to the mourning cloak's bold, simple design.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its close relative the Mourning Cloak, the Compton Tortoiseshell is smaller, has much more orange coloration, and sports those signature scalloped wing edges instead of the Mourning Cloak's smooth margins.
